sources: Clemson University Home & Garden Information Center, Velvet Ants: wasps (Mutillidae), not ants; eastern velvet ant about 3/4 inch; dense velvety fuzz with bold warning colors; wingless females deliver a severe, very painful sting; winged males are harmless; nicknamed 'cow killers' but no record of a cow ever killed; squeak by rubbing two abdominal segments together; exoskeleton so tough that chemical and mechanical control rarely work; parasitize ground-nesting bees and wasps, laying eggs on the host's immature stages, which the developing velvet ant consumes until the host dies; adults feed on flower nectar; https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/velvet-ants/

Science News (2025), Velvet ants have the Swiss Army knife of venoms (Borjon et al., Current Biology; Indiana University, University of Queensland, Utah State): scarlet velvet ant venom has 24 peptides, some targeting insect neurons and some causing pain in mammals; Justin Schmidt described the sting as 'hot oil from the deep fryer spilling over your entire hand'; extremely tough exoskeleton; mammals, reptiles, amphibians and birds react to the sting; nothing seems to consistently eat velvet ants; https://sciencenews.org/?p=3147950

beats.say: This fuzzy red ant is actually a wasp. And they call it the cow killer.
The velvet ant. No wings, and covered in red and black fuzz.
Only the females are wingless. The males can fly, but can't sting.
Her venom is a mix of twenty-four different ingredients.
One scientist said the sting feels like hot oil from a deep fryer, spilling over your whole hand.
But relax. There's no record of it ever killing a cow.
